slides.misconceptions: Pupils may think any two parts make halves, even if the parts are different sizes. Reinforce that equal parts must be the same size. A quarter is one of four equal parts, not one of four unequal parts.
slides.background: The words half and quarter describe equal shares: half means one of two equal parts, and quarter means one of four. The parts do not have to be the same shape, but they must have equal size.
slides.run: Spend about 4 minutes. Read the definitions together. Ask pupils to point to one half and one quarter in the diagrams, then explain what makes the parts equal.

answers: One of 4 equal parts is shaded.
slides.misconceptions: Choosing the first option shows pupils may think a shaded part is a quarter whenever there are two parts; that is a half. Choosing the third shows they may ignore whether the parts are equal. A quarter is one of four equal parts.
slides.run: Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils choose independently, then compare with a partner and explain why the parts must be equal.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may count both groups and answer 8, rather than counting one group. Emphasise that half of 8 is the number in one of the two equal groups: 4.
slides.background: Sharing into two equal groups is a practical way to find half. Each counter belongs to one group, so the two group totals are equal and together make the starting amount.
slides.run: Spend about 5 minutes. Model sharing the counters one at a time between two groups. Count one group together and check that both groups have 4.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may answer 10 by counting all the counters, or make unequal groups and still call one group half. Share one counter at a time between two groups; each group has 5.
slides.run: Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils work alone with counters or a drawing, share 10 into two equal groups and write how many are in one group. Check answers together.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may count all 12 counters, or share them into two groups and call one group a quarter. A quarter needs four equal groups; one group has 3.
slides.background: Finding a quarter of a set means dividing the whole set into four equal groups and taking the amount in one group. This is also one way to calculate 12 ÷ 4.
slides.run: Spend about 5 minutes. Model sharing 12 counters one at a time into four groups. Count one group together and check that the four groups total 12.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may make two groups, or count all 16 instead of one of four equal groups. Share 16 into four equal groups; there are 4 in each group.
slides.run: Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils work alone or in pairs with counters or drawings. They make four equal groups, count one group and record the answer.

slides.misconceptions: Choosing the first option shows pupils are finding a half, not a quarter. Choosing the third shows they know to make four groups but count the whole amount rather than one group. One quarter of 8 is one of four equal groups.
slides.run: Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils select a method independently, then justify their choice to a partner. Invite the class to use the method to find a quarter of 8.

answers: A is one half; B is one quarter.
slides.misconceptions: Pupils may name a fraction by the shape or direction of the dividing line rather than by the number of equal parts and the number shaded. Check that the parts are equal: one of two is a half, and one of four is a quarter.
slides.background: A diagonal line can split a square into two equal triangles. A rectangle split into four equal horizontal strips has four equal parts. The fraction depends on how many equal parts there are and how many are shaded.
slides.run: Spend about 5 minutes. Pupils write the name of each shaded fraction and explain their reasoning to a partner. Ask a few pupils to say how the number of equal parts helped them decide.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may count the whole set instead of one group, or make the wrong number of groups. For half, share into two equal groups; for a quarter, share into four equal groups, then count one group.
slides.background: The answers can be checked by combining the equal groups: two groups of 9 make 18; four groups of 2 make 8; and four groups of 5 make 20.
slides.run: Spend about 8 minutes. Pupils draw counters and circle two equal groups for the half, then four equal groups for each quarter. They write the number in one group as each answer. Review one example together.

answers: Half of 16 is 8; a quarter of 16 is 4. Half is more.
slides.misconceptions: For the birds, pupils may give 7 as the number that fly away rather than the number that stay; half of 14 fly away, so the other half, 7, stay. For the buns, sharing into two groups finds a half, not a quarter; four plates need four equal groups of 3. In the stretch, pupils may think the quarter is larger because the number 4 is mentioned; compare the amounts, 8 and 4.
slides.background: These problems apply equal sharing to everyday contexts. In the bird question, the remaining birds are the other equal half. In the bun question, fair sharing means every plate gets the same number.
slides.run: Spend about 10 minutes. Pupils draw or use counters to solve the first two problems, then complete the stretch if ready. Ask them to explain how their equal groups show each answer.
